Part 1 Concepts and methods

Study one topic at a time. Each chapter combines its core concepts and method reference with short scenarios that show the input, Java code, output and reason for the result. These short Java snippets belong inside a main method; standard Java imports are assumed. Complete runnable programs for the worked coding answers are included in the download.

1.01 Objects constructors and immutability

Concept

An object is an instance with state and behaviour. Object, in java.lang, is the root class inherited by Java classes. Objects, in java.util, is a separate utility class containing static methods such as Objects.equals() and Objects.requireNonNull(). Order and Trade are application domain types. The plural utility class does not create trading objects for you.

ConceptMeaningTrading or automation example
EncapsulationControl access to state through a class's APIPrivate order fields and validated construction
AbstractionExpose a useful contract without its implementation detailsA RiskCheck interface with an evaluate method
InheritanceA class extends another class and inherits accessible behaviourA specialised result type; avoid inheritance solely to share test state
PolymorphismAn interface or superclass reference can invoke an implementation's overridden methodDifferent RiskCheck implementations behind the same interface
CompositionAn object delegates work to collaborators it holdsA test service composed of a client, parser and comparator
OverloadingSame method name with different parameter listsfindOrder(String id) and findOrder(long sequence)
OverridingA subtype supplies an implementation of an inherited instance methodOrder.equals(Object)

Overloading is resolved from compile-time types. Overridden instance methods use runtime dispatch. Static methods are hidden rather than overridden; constructors are not inherited. An interface describes a contract and can also declare default and static methods. An abstract class can hold instance state and constructors as well as abstract and concrete methods. A class can implement several interfaces but extend only one class.

Constructors and this

A constructor initialises a new object and has the same name as its class, with no return type. In this.symbol = symbol, this.symbol is the object field and symbol is the parameter. A static method has no current object represented by this. A final field cannot be reassigned after initialisation; a final reference alone does not make a mutable object immutable.

Encapsulation and safe object design

Java passes arguments by value. For objects, that value is a reference: a method can mutate a shared mutable object, but reassigning its parameter does not reassign the caller's variable. == compares reference identity for ordinary objects; use appropriate value equality for content.

A record automatically supplies a canonical constructor, component accessors, equals(), hashCode() and toString(). Its default equality uses every component. A record containing BigDecimal therefore inherits scale-sensitive BigDecimal equality unless you define a different domain rule. A record containing a mutable List is not deeply immutable merely because the record's reference fields are final.

In a defensive-copy constructor, storing an unmodifiable copy protects the saved list structure from changes through the input list. This is a shallow copy. It is sufficient for immutable String elements; mutable elements require an appropriate deeper-copy strategy. List.copyOf() rejects null elements.

Exceptions and resource ownership

Use IllegalArgumentException for an invalid argument contract, and understand that requireNonNull() throws NullPointerException. Checked exceptions must be handled or declared; unchecked exceptions are RuntimeException subtypes. Try-with-resources closes AutoCloseable resources in reverse declaration order. A return inside finally can suppress an exception, so avoid that pattern. A static shared test object can retain data across tests even when each test's local variables have disappeared.

Scenario Create a trade

A trade must retain the symbol supplied when the object is constructed.

Input

text
Symbol supplied to the constructor: AAPL

Java

java
final class Trade {
    private final String symbol;
    Trade(String symbol) { this.symbol = symbol; }
    String symbol() { return symbol; }
}
Trade trade = new Trade("AAPL");
System.out.println(trade.symbol());

Output

text
AAPL

Why this happens

The constructor stores the parameter on that particular object. The getter reads the stored field.

Scenario Reject an invalid quantity

An order constructor should reject a zero or negative quantity before assigning fields.

Input

text
Quantity: -1

Java

java
try {
    int quantity = -1;
    if (quantity <= 0) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Quantity must be positive");
    }
} catch (IllegalArgumentException error) {
    System.out.println(error.getMessage());
}

Output

text
Quantity must be positive

Why this happens

The guard fails immediately. Use quantity < 0 instead if the contract permits zero.

Scenario Protect order tags from caller changes

A caller changes its original list after an immutable order snapshot has copied it.

Input

text
Original tags: [BUY]
Caller later appends: CHANGED

Java

java
List<String> input = new ArrayList<>(List.of("BUY"));
List<String> stored = List.copyOf(input);
input.add("CHANGED");
System.out.println(input);
System.out.println(stored);

Output

text
[BUY, CHANGED]
[BUY]

Why this happens

List.copyOf creates an unmodifiable structural snapshot. It is a shallow copy; mutable elements would need their own copying policy.

1.02 Equality null handling and Object utility methods

Concept

Reference identity asks whether two references point to the same object. Logical equality asks whether two values meet the domain equality rule. Hash-based collections require equal objects to have equal hashes. Matching hashes alone do not prove equality.

Object methods

MethodPurposeInterview point
equals(Object)Logical equality when overriddenThe inherited implementation uses identity
hashCode()Hash value used by hash collectionsEqual objects need equal hashes; collisions are permitted
toString()Text representationMake diagnostics useful without exposing secrets
getClass()Runtime classUnderstand exact-type checks versus instanceof
wait() and timed waitWait on this object's monitorOwn the monitor; recheck a condition in a loop
notify() / notifyAll()Wake monitor waitersWaking does not transfer the lock immediately
clone()Cloning mechanism when supportedNot a general public deep-copy operation

Know equals() as an equivalence relation: reflexive, symmetric, transitive and consistent, with false for null. Do not use a mutable field in equality or hashing while the object is stored in a HashMap or HashSet. A hash code is neither a unique identifier nor a guaranteed memory address. Prefer explicit copy constructors or factories over introducing clone() in a new domain design. Finalization is deprecated for removal and should not be used for executor or browser cleanup.

Objects utility methods

MethodExampleKey behaviour
equals(a, b)Objects.equals(orderId, otherId)Null-safe equality
hash(values...)Objects.hash(orderId)Hash multiple equality fields consistently
hashCode(value)Objects.hashCode(orderId)One object's hash or zero for null
requireNonNull(value, message)Objects.requireNonNull(trade, "trade")Throws NullPointerException
requireNonNullElse(value, fallback)Objects.requireNonNullElse(symbol, "UNKNOWN")Non-null fallback when value is null
requireNonNullElseGet(value, supplier)Objects.requireNonNullElseGet(value, factory)Fallback is produced only if needed
isNull(value) / nonNull(value)stream.filter(Objects::nonNull)Useful predicates when the data contract permits filtering nulls
toString(value, fallback)Objects.toString(value, "missing")Null-safe diagnostic text
deepEquals(a, b)Objects.deepEquals(array1, array2)Handles array-content comparison; not arbitrary recursive domain equality

Objects.hash(id) and Objects.hashCode(id) need not return the same number. Choose a consistent implementation; equal instances must use the same rule. Filtering away invalid records is a business decision, not an automatic alternative to validation.

Null blank and short circuiting

null means there is no String object. isBlank() checks an existing string and returns true when it is empty or contains only Java-defined whitespace.

Valuevalue == nullvalue.isBlank()
nulltrueThrows NullPointerException
""falsetrue
" "falsetrue
"\t\n"falsetrue
"T1"falsefalse
" T1 "falsefalse

Java evaluates || from left to right and skips the right expression if the left is true. This protects the method call when tradeId is null. In a price check, price == null || price.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0 rejects a missing, zero or negative price.

Changing that price check to && changes its meaning and breaks null safety: if price is null, the right expression is evaluated and throws NullPointerException; if price is non-null, the left expression is false and the price comparison is skipped.

Scenario Compare optional identifiers safely

An optional API identifier is missing; compare it without calling a method on null.

Input

text
first = null
second = T1

Java

java
String first = null;
String second = "T1";
System.out.println(Objects.equals(first, second));
System.out.println(Objects.equals(first, null));
System.out.println(Objects.requireNonNullElse(first, "UNKNOWN"));
System.out.println(Objects.toString(first, "missing"));

Output

text
false
true
UNKNOWN
missing

Why this happens

Objects.equals handles nulls. requireNonNullElse supplies a fallback for null, not for a blank string. toString supplies readable diagnostic text.

Scenario Validate null and blank IDs

Reject missing or blank trade IDs while accepting an actual ID.

Input

text
IDs: null, empty string, T1

Java

java
for (String id : Arrays.asList(null, "", "T1")) {
    System.out.println(id == null || id.isBlank());
}

Output

text
true
true
false

Why this happens

When id is null, the left side of OR is true, so isBlank is skipped. This prevents NullPointerException.

Scenario Remove duplicate value objects

A trade-ID value object defines identity using its single record component.

Input

text
Trade IDs: T1, T1, T2

Java

java
record TradeId(String value) {}
TradeId first = new TradeId("T1");
TradeId duplicate = new TradeId("T1");
System.out.println(first == duplicate);
System.out.println(first.equals(duplicate));
System.out.println(new HashSet<>(List.of(first, duplicate, new TradeId("T2"))).size());

Output

text
false
true
2

Why this happens

The two T1 objects have different identities, but record equality and hashing use their component value. HashSet therefore stores one T1 and one T2.

1.03 BigDecimal financial arithmetic and rounding

Concept

BigDecimal represents arbitrary-precision decimal values with explicit scale and rounding control. Construct prices directly from strings, such as new BigDecimal("100.25"). Constructing from a double can preserve its binary floating-point approximation.

Common methods are add(), subtract(), multiply(), divide(), compareTo(), signum(), setScale(), scale(), precision() and toPlainString(). For 10.50, scale is 2 and precision is 4. Scale can be negative for other representations; do not treat it as an unsigned count in every possible BigDecimal.

Arithmetic returns a value without changing the original object. total.add(price) discards that returned result; total = total.add(price) keeps it. Exact division such as 1 / 3 throws ArithmeticException unless an appropriate precision or rounding rule is supplied. In divide(divisor, 2, HALF_UP), 2 specifies two decimal places.

equals() compares numeric value and scale. compareTo() compares numerical value. Consequently 10.0 and 10.00 are unequal under equals() but compareTo() returns zero. ZERO, ONE and TEN are useful constants.

Important methods

MethodMeaning
new BigDecimal(String)Construct directly from decimal text
BigDecimal.valueOf(long)Convert an integral quantity
add(), subtract(), multiply()Return the arithmetic result without changing the original value
divide(divisor)Exact division when the result is representable
divide(divisor, scale, roundingMode)Apply an explicit division and rounding contract
compareTo(), equals()Numeric comparison versus value-and-scale equality
signum()Negative, zero or positive
setScale(), scale(), precision()Set representation scale or inspect scale and significant digits
toPlainString()Produce text without exponent notation

Scenario Calculate order notional

An executed order has a decimal price and an integral quantity.

Input

text
Price: 100.25
Quantity: 10

Java

java
BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("100.25");
int quantity = 10;
BigDecimal notional = price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(quantity));
System.out.println(notional.toPlainString());

Output

text
1002.50

Why this happens

Convert the quantity to BigDecimal, multiply and keep the returned result. No binary floating-point arithmetic is introduced.

Scenario Keep the updated total

A running notional total must retain the result of addition.

Input

text
Initial total: 0
Notional to add: 100.25

Java

java
BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.ZERO;
BigDecimal notional = new BigDecimal("100.25");
total.add(notional);
System.out.println(total);
total = total.add(notional);
System.out.println(total);

Output

text
0
100.25

Why this happens

The first result is discarded because BigDecimal is immutable. The assignment keeps the new value.

Scenario Compare representation and round a ratio

Two systems use different decimal scales, and a report requires a rounded one-third ratio.

Input

text
Values: 10.0 and 10.00
Ratio: 1 / 3, two decimal places, HALF_UP

Java

java
BigDecimal first = new BigDecimal("10.0");
BigDecimal second = new BigDecimal("10.00");
System.out.println(first.equals(second));
System.out.println(first.compareTo(second) == 0);
System.out.println(BigDecimal.ONE.divide(new BigDecimal("3"), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP));

Output

text
false
true
0.33

Why this happens

equals includes scale; compareTo tests numeric value. The division specifies its rounding policy because one-third has no finite exact decimal representation.

1.04 Collections lists sets queues and copies

Concept and implementation choice

Collection is an interface for groups of elements. Collections is a utility class with static operations. Map is part of the collections framework but does not extend Collection. List preserves positional order and permits duplicates; Set models uniqueness; Queue and Deque model processing order.

ImplementationOrdering and typical costTrading use
ArrayListIndexed get O(1), append amortised O(1), middle insert/remove O(n)Trade snapshots and reports
LinkedListIndexed access O(n); efficient end operationsKnow its trade-offs; ArrayDeque often suits queues better
HashSetExpected O(1) membership; no encounter-order guaranteeExecution-ID membership
LinkedHashSetExpected O(1) membership; insertion orderDeduplication that retains first occurrence order
TreeSetO(log n) operations; comparator-based uniquenessSorted distinct values with an agreed comparator
HashMapExpected O(1) key lookup/update; no order guaranteeTrade lookup by immutable ID
LinkedHashMapDefined insertion order or optional access orderDeterministic output or a small access-order cache
TreeMapO(log n) get/put/remove; sorted keysOrdered price levels
ArrayDequeAmortised O(1) operations at either end; rejects nullFIFO event buffering or a stack
PriorityQueueOffer/poll O(log n), peek O(1); iteration is not sortedTrack a small top-N set
EnumMapKeys belong to one enum typeCounts by execution status
ConcurrentHashMapConcurrent keyed access; no null keys/valuesConcurrent counters or quote caches
CopyOnWriteArrayListSnapshot traversal; updates copy the backing arrayA small listener list with many reads and few writes

Ordinary ArrayList, HashMap, TreeMap and HashSet are not thread-safe. Complexity statements assume the usual implementation and appropriate hashing; do not describe every HashMap operation as guaranteed O(1). A fail-fast iterator is a bug-detection aid, not a concurrency guarantee.

Important methods

MethodMeaning or common trap
add(value), addAll(values)Append/add elements when supported
contains(value)Value membership; cost depends on implementation
remove(value)Remove a matching value when supported
removeIf(predicate)Remove all matching elements when supported
size(), isEmpty(), clear()Basic inspection and mutation
iterator(), iterator.remove()Controlled traversal and supported removal
get(index), set(index,value)List positional access and replacement
remove(index)List overload removes by index
sort(comparator), replaceAll(operator)List sorting or transformation in place
subList(from,to)Backed list view, not an independent copy
retainAll(values), removeAll(values)Intersection-style retention or removal
toArray(String[]::new)Produce a typed array
List.of(), Set.of(), copyOf()Unmodifiable factories; understand null and uniqueness rules

For List<Integer>, remove(1) removes index 1; remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes the value 1. Avoid structural modification through the collection during an enhanced for-loop. Use an appropriate iterator or removeIf() when removal is intended.

Utilities factories and views

Collections.sort(), reverse(), frequency(), disjoint(), min() and max() operate on collections under their respective preconditions. Collections.binarySearch() requires a list already sorted with the same ordering. Collections.unmodifiableList(backing) is a read-only view that still reflects backing-list changes. List.copyOf(backing) gives an unmodifiable snapshot of the list structure. Both may still contain references to mutable objects, although copyOf rejects null elements.

Arrays.asList() is fixed-size and backed by its array. List.of() is unmodifiable. Set.of() rejects duplicate elements and nulls; Map.of() rejects duplicate keys and null keys/values. Arrays.asList(new int[]{1,2}) makes a one-element List<int[]> rather than a list of boxed integers. Use Arrays.stream(numbers).boxed() to box primitive int elements.

Scenario Keep unique IDs in encounter order

A report should display each execution ID once in the order first seen.

Input

text
IDs: [E2, E1, E2]

Java

java
List<String> input = List.of("E2", "E1", "E2");
List<String> unique = new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(input));
System.out.println(unique);
System.out.println(unique.contains("E1"));

Output

text
[E2, E1]
true

Why this happens

LinkedHashSet combines uniqueness with insertion order. ArrayList provides the required list result.

Scenario Distinguish removing an index from a value

A list of integer quantities has two remove overloads.

Input

text
Quantities: [10, 20, 10]

Java

java
List<Integer> quantities = new ArrayList<>(List.of(10, 20, 10));
quantities.remove(1);
System.out.println(quantities);
quantities.remove(Integer.valueOf(10));
System.out.println(quantities);

Output

text
[10, 10]
[10]

Why this happens

remove(1) removes index 1. Wrapping the argument as Integer selects removal of the matching value.

Scenario Understand a fixed-size list

A test fixture created with Arrays.asList permits replacement but not a size change.

Input

text
IDs: [T1, T2]
Replace index 0 with T0; then try to append T3

Java

java
List<String> ids = Arrays.asList("T1", "T2");
ids.set(0, "T0");
System.out.println(ids);
try { ids.add("T3"); }
catch (UnsupportedOperationException error) { System.out.println("Fixed size"); }

Output

text
[T0, T2]
Fixed size

Why this happens

Arrays.asList is backed by an array and has fixed size. Use a new ArrayList when the result must grow.

Scenario Process events in FIFO order

A small event buffer should return the oldest queued event first.

Input

text
Events offered: E1, then E2

Java

java
Deque<String> events = new ArrayDeque<>();
events.offerLast("E1");
events.offerLast("E2");
System.out.println(events.pollFirst());
System.out.println(events.peekFirst());

Output

text
E1
E2

Why this happens

pollFirst removes the head, while peekFirst reads the next head without removing it.

1.05 Maps sorted maps and comparators

Concept

A Map associates one value with each key. Choose the key from stable business identity, such as trade ID. HashMap supports efficient keyed access, LinkedHashMap gives a defined encounter order, and TreeMap sorts keys. A concurrent map has different atomicity guarantees from an ordinary map.

Important methods

MethodTrading example or behaviour
put(key,value), get(key)Store or retrieve an order by ID
containsKey(key)Distinguish absence from a stored null where null is allowed
getOrDefault(key,defaultValue)Read a fallback; it does not insert
putIfAbsent(key,value)Initialise only when absent or mapped to null
computeIfAbsent(key,function)Create a per-symbol bucket or value when missing
merge(key,value,function)Initialise or combine a non-null value
compute(key,function)Recompute from the current mapping; null result removes it
replace(key,value), replace(key,old,new)Replace an existing mapping, optionally conditionally
remove(key), remove(key,value)Remove a mapping, optionally conditionally
keySet(), values(), entrySet()Backed views of keys, values or entries
forEach(action), replaceAll(function)Visit or update entries

The short scenarios below use ordinary HashMap in a single thread. Atomicity guarantees depend on the implementation. ConcurrentHashMap supplies atomic keyed updates, but a mutable ArrayList stored as a map value does not become thread-safe merely because the map is concurrent. Keep compute functions short, avoid remote calls inside them, and do not recursively modify the same map from their remapping functions.

Sorted price levels and comparator contracts

NavigableMap methods firstEntry(), lastEntry(), floorEntry(), ceilingEntry(), lowerEntry() and higherEntry() locate boundary or neighbouring prices. With ascending price keys, the highest bid is lastEntry() and the lowest ask is firstEntry(). Empty maps return null for firstEntry()/lastEntry(). Prefer integral ticks or a clearly defined price-key representation.

TreeMap and TreeSet decide key equality using their comparator or natural comparison. BigDecimal("10.0") and BigDecimal("10.00") compare numerically equal, so a TreeSet groups them at one position even though equals() is false. HashSet uses equals()/hashCode() and treats those representations as distinct. Understand this contract difference before choosing decimal map keys.

Comparator.comparing(), comparingLong(), thenComparing(), reversed() and nullsLast() are useful. Reverse the price comparator before adding an ascending trade-ID tie-breaker; reversing the complete combined comparator reverses both criteria. Use Integer.compare/Long.compare instead of subtraction, which may overflow.

Scenario Accumulate quantity using getOrDefault

Two AAPL trades contribute quantities to the same symbol total.

Input

text
Existing total: no AAPL entry
Incoming quantities: 100, then 200

Java

java
Map<String, Integer> totals = new HashMap<>();
totals.put("AAPL", totals.getOrDefault("AAPL", 0) + 100);
totals.put("AAPL", totals.getOrDefault("AAPL", 0) + 200);
System.out.println(totals.get("AAPL"));
System.out.println(totals.getOrDefault("MSFT", 0));
System.out.println(totals.containsKey("MSFT"));

Output

text
300
0
false

Why this happens

getOrDefault only reads a value or a fallback. put stores the updated total; the MSFT fallback does not create an entry.

Scenario Use merge and computeIfAbsent

Count AAPL executions and collect their IDs into a symbol bucket.

Input

text
Executions: E1 and E2 for AAPL

Java

java
Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
counts.merge("AAPL", 1, Integer::sum);
counts.merge("AAPL", 1, Integer::sum);
Map<String, List<String>> ids = new HashMap<>();
ids.computeIfAbsent("AAPL", symbol -> new ArrayList<>()).add("E1");
ids.computeIfAbsent("AAPL", symbol -> new ArrayList<>()).add("E2");
System.out.println(counts.get("AAPL"));
System.out.println(ids.get("AAPL"));

Output

text
2
[E1, E2]

Why this happens

merge inserts or combines a value. computeIfAbsent creates a list only when needed and then returns the current list.

Scenario Find the best bid and a neighbouring price

An ascending TreeMap stores bid levels in integral price ticks.

Input

text
Bids: 10000 -> 10, 10025 -> 20
Neighbour query: floor of 10010

Java

java
NavigableMap<Long, Long> bids = new TreeMap<>();
bids.put(10000L, 10L);
bids.put(10025L, 20L);
System.out.println(bids.lastEntry().getKey());
System.out.println(bids.floorEntry(10010L).getKey());

Output

text
10025
10000

Why this happens

The highest bid is the last entry. floorEntry returns the greatest key no higher than the requested price.

1.06 Streams pipelines filtering mapping and ordering

Concept

A Stream describes a processing pipeline over a source; it does not store elements like a collection. A typical trading pipeline selects eligible records, transforms them to notionals and collects or reduces the result. Prefer a readable loop when a pipeline obscures ordering, error handling or mutable state.

InterfaceShapeExample
Predicate<T>T to booleantrade -> trade.status() == EXECUTED
Function<T,R>T to RTrade::symbol
Consumer<T>T to no returned valueA controlled output action
Supplier<T>No argument to TArrayList::new
BinaryOperator<T>Two T values to TBigDecimal::add

A method reference is shorthand for a compatible lambda. Trade::symbol corresponds to trade -> trade.symbol(). A lambda's captured local variables must be final or effectively final; mutating an object referenced by such a variable may still be possible and may still be unsafe.

Intermediate methods

OperationPurposeTrading example
filter(predicate)Keep matching elementsExecuted BUY trades
map(function)Transform one element to one valueTrade to notional
flatMap(function)Flatten each nested streamBatches of executions to one execution stream
distinct()Deduplicate by element equalityExact duplicate objects under their equality contract
sorted(comparator)Order elementsNotional descending with an ID tie-break
limit(n), skip(n)Restrict or skip encounter positionsA small report page after ordering
peek(action)Observe a pipeline during debuggingDo not put required audit writes here
mapToInt(), mapToLong(), mapToDouble()Primitive streamsIntegral quantities or counts

Intermediate operations are lazy. Some operations, including sorted(), need buffering. distinct() uses the element's equals/hashCode semantics, so it does not deduplicate records by one chosen field automatically.

Terminal methods

OperationResult or behaviour
collect(collector)A collection or grouped result
reduce(identity, accumulator)Combine into a value such as BigDecimal total
toList()Unmodifiable List, available since Java 16
count()long number of elements
min(comparator), max(comparator)Optional element
findFirst(), findAny()Optional element under their ordering semantics
anyMatch(), allMatch(), noneMatch()Short-circuiting boolean queries
forEach(), forEachOrdered()Terminal actions with different order guarantees

A stream is consumed once; create a new stream for another traversal. findAny() need not return the first encounter element, particularly in parallel. On an empty stream, anyMatch() is false while allMatch() and noneMatch() are true. Do not use Optional.get() without establishing presence. Use orElse(), orElseGet() or orElseThrow() according to the contract; orElseGet() produces its fallback lazily.

Reduction and parallel execution contracts

An identity must be neutral for the operation, such as zero for addition. A reduction operation must be associative for correct regrouping, and its functions must obey the stream contracts. Exact BigDecimal addition without intermediate rounding is suitable for summation; introducing rounding at every addition can make regrouping change results. Floating-point summation can also vary with grouping.

parallelStream() does not guarantee faster execution. Consider data size, CPU work, splitting cost, ordering, shared resources and blocking. Avoid shared ArrayList.add() or a mutable external total inside parallel forEach(). Built-in collectors manage their own accumulation and combination rather than requiring you to mutate one shared result container. forEachOrdered() preserves encounter order for actions but does not make arbitrary shared state generally thread-safe.

Do not depend on peek() or another intermediate operation for required logging, persistence or audit events: an implementation can omit some operations when it can derive the terminal result without them. Required effects should be designed explicitly outside such optimisation-sensitive stages.

Scenario Select executed trade IDs

A report includes only executed trades and displays their IDs.

Input

text
T1 EXECUTED, T2 PENDING, T3 EXECUTED

Java

java
record Trade(String id, String status) {}
List<Trade> trades = List.of(new Trade("T1", "EXECUTED"),
    new Trade("T2", "PENDING"), new Trade("T3", "EXECUTED"));
List<String> ids = trades.stream()
    .filter(t -> t.status().equals("EXECUTED"))
    .map(Trade::id).toList();
System.out.println(ids);

Output

text
[T1, T3]

Why this happens

filter selects matching records. map transforms each remaining record to its ID. toList triggers processing and returns an unmodifiable result.

Scenario Flatten execution batches

Two received batches should become one ordered stream of execution IDs.

Input

text
Batches: [[E1, E2], [E3]]

Java

java
List<List<String>> batches = List.of(List.of("E1", "E2"), List.of("E3"));
List<String> ids = batches.stream().flatMap(List::stream).toList();
System.out.println(ids);

Output

text
[E1, E2, E3]

Why this happens

flatMap converts each inner list into a stream and joins those streams into one sequence.

Scenario Show the top two prices

A report displays the largest two prices, represented here as integral ticks.

Input

text
Prices: [10050, 10025, 10075]
Limit: 2

Java

java
List<Long> prices = List.of(10050L, 10025L, 10075L);
System.out.println(prices.stream().sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).limit(2).toList());

Output

text
[10075, 10050]

Why this happens

sorted arranges descending values before limit selects the report size. A stable tie-breaker is needed when sorting domain objects with equal primary values.

1.07 Collectors grouping and financial reductions

Concept

A collector describes how to build an aggregate result. A classifier chooses a group; a downstream collector decides what to compute within that group. Use decimal reduction for money rather than converting monetary values to double.

Important collectors

CollectorTypical use
toList(), toSet(), toCollection(ArrayList::new)Collect elements; request a specific implementation when needed
toMap(key,value,merge)Index trades with an explicit duplicate-key rule
groupingBy(classifier)Group executions by symbol
mapping(mapper,downstream)Transform grouped elements
reducing(identity,mapper,operator)Aggregate BigDecimal values per group
counting(), summingLong()Counts or integral quantity totals
partitioningBy(predicate)Both boolean groups, such as accepted versus rejected
joining(delimiter)Diagnostic ID text
collectingAndThen(downstream,finisher)Apply a final conversion
maxBy(comparator), minBy(comparator)Optional extrema per group

Collectors.toList() does not specify a concrete list implementation or mutability guarantee. Stream.toList() is unmodifiable. Use toCollection(ArrayList::new) when a mutable ArrayList is explicitly required. toMap() without a merge function fails on duplicate keys; choose whether duplicates are errors, first-wins, latest-wins or combined values. A plain groupingBy result has no general insertion-order guarantee; supply an appropriate map factory when order matters.

For symbol grouping, the classifier chooses the symbol bucket. The mapper computes each trade's notional. The downstream reduction adds those values starting at zero. BigDecimal is appropriate for exact decimal money calculations; averagingDouble() is not a substitute for a specified decimal VWAP calculation.

Scenario Count executions per symbol

A dashboard counts how many execution records belong to each symbol.

Input

text
Symbols: [AAPL, MSFT, AAPL]

Java

java
List<String> symbols = List.of("AAPL", "MSFT", "AAPL");
Map<String, Long> counts = symbols.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(
    symbol -> symbol, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting()));
System.out.println(counts);

Output

text
{AAPL=2, MSFT=1}

Why this happens

groupingBy creates a bucket per symbol and counting totals its elements. The TreeMap factory makes the printed key order deterministic.

Scenario Define a duplicate-key policy

Two execution records must be counted rather than failing on the same symbol key.

Input

text
Symbols: [AAPL, AAPL]

Java

java
Map<String, Integer> counts = Stream.of("AAPL", "AAPL").collect(
    Collectors.toMap(symbol -> symbol, symbol -> 1, Integer::sum));
System.out.println(counts);

Output

text
{AAPL=2}

Why this happens

The third toMap argument combines duplicate keys. Omitting it would throw IllegalStateException for this input.

Scenario Reduce decimal notionals

Two already-calculated notionals must be summed exactly.

Input

text
Notionals: 1002.50 and 510.00

Java

java
BigDecimal total = Stream.of(new BigDecimal("1002.50"), new BigDecimal("510.00"))
    .reduce(BigDecimal.ZERO, BigDecimal::add);
System.out.println(total.toPlainString());

Output

text
1512.50

Why this happens

Zero is the identity for addition. The reduction returns zero for an empty stream and preserves decimal precision without intermediate rounding.

1.08 Threads executors futures and lifecycle management

Concept

Concurrency means tasks can make progress during overlapping periods. Parallelism means work actually executes simultaneously. A trading test runner may use concurrency for independent checks, but correctness still depends on data ownership, atomic updates, visibility and ordering.

ConceptMeaningExample
Race conditionCorrectness depends on an uncontrolled interleavingTwo workers lose a read-modify-write counter increment
AtomicityAn operation behaves indivisibly at its specified scopeAtomicLong.incrementAndGet()
VisibilityOne thread can reliably observe another's published writesProper volatile, lock or future-completion coordination
OrderingDefined relationships constrain observation of actionsTask effects are visible after successful Future.get()
Mutual exclusionOne thread enters a protected critical section at a timeOne lock protects a multi-field invariant
DeadlockThreads wait in a cycle for resources held by one anotherWorkers acquire two account locks in opposite orders
StarvationA task repeatedly fails to obtain needed execution/resourcesA poorly controlled or saturated executor
BackpressureProducers are slowed or rejected when capacity is reachedA bounded execution-event queue

volatile gives visibility/ordering guarantees for accesses to that field; it does not make count++ atomic. synchronized supplies monitor-based mutual exclusion and visibility when all participants use the same locking protocol. Atomic operations apply at their documented scope, not automatically across several unrelated fields or map keys. A cross-account transfer or consistent multi-symbol snapshot needs an appropriate wider protocol.

Methods and lifecycle

Runnable returns no result and cannot declare checked exceptions in run(). Callable<T> returns T and may throw checked exceptions. Calling Thread.start() schedules a new thread; calling run() directly is an ordinary method call on the caller's thread. A Thread instance can be started once.

Method or APIInterview point
Thread.start(), join()Start execution; wait for a thread to finish
Thread.sleep(...)Pauses current thread; does not release owned monitors
interrupt(), isInterrupted()Request interruption; inspect its flag
Thread.interrupted()Checks and clears the current thread's flag
ExecutorService.submit(...)Schedule a task and obtain a Future
execute(Runnable)Schedule without returning a Future
Future.get() / get(timeout,unit)Obtain result or observe failure/timeout
Future.cancel(true)Request cancellation and possible interruption
invokeAll(tasks,timeout,unit)Wait for a batch under a shared timeout and cancel unfinished tasks
shutdown()Reject new tasks and allow submitted work to finish
shutdownNow()Attempt interruption and return waiting tasks that never started
awaitTermination(timeout,unit)Wait for termination; does not itself start shutdown

Thread states are NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING and TERMINATED. A runnable thread is not guaranteed to be currently using a CPU. Cancellation is cooperative; a task ignoring interruption may continue. A timed Future.get() does not automatically cancel the task. A submitted task's failure is typically observed as ExecutionException from get(); do not discard futures and assume every task succeeded.

If InterruptedException is propagated, let the caller handle it. If it is caught without propagation, restore interruption with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and normally stop the affected work. Avoid swallowing interruption or turning a cancellation into a successful trading result.

Deadlines and cleanup

Choose a pool size from the work and resource limits rather than one thread per trade. newFixedThreadPool() limits active workers but uses an unbounded work queue; a production producer may need a bounded ThreadPoolExecutor and an explicit rejection policy. For one overall deadline, track the remaining budget with System.nanoTime() or use a suitable timed batch API. Giving each future its own full timeout multiplies the total potential wait.

The runnable examples target Java 17 and therefore manage executor shutdown explicitly. ExecutorService became AutoCloseable after Java 17; do not assume Java 21 try-with-resources examples compile on Java 17. Virtual threads are a Java 21 topic: they can help workloads that spend time blocked, but do not make shared state safe or increase CPU capacity for compute-bound work.

Monitor coordination

Own an object's monitor before calling wait(), notify() or notifyAll(). A guarded wait uses while(conditionNotMet) wait(), because wakeups can be spurious and another thread may change the condition before the waiter reacquires the lock. wait() releases that object's monitor while waiting; sleep() does not. Prefer higher-level constructs when they match the problem. In tests, coordinate workers with a latch and await futures; do not use arbitrary sleeps as proof of completion.

Scenario Obtain a simulated risk result

Run one independent calculation on an executor and wait for its result.

Input

text
Risk result produced by the task: 150.25

Java

java
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
try {
    Future<BigDecimal> result = pool.submit(() -> new BigDecimal("150.25"));
    System.out.println(result.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
} finally {
    pool.shutdownNow();
}

Output

text
150.25

Why this happens

submit returns a Future. get retrieves its value and observes failures. The executor is shut down by its owner in finally.

Scenario Observe a worker failure

A task rejects an invalid risk input; the caller must not silently ignore that failure.

Input

text
Task throws IllegalArgumentException with message Risk input invalid

Java

java
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
try {
    Future<Integer> result = pool.submit(() -> {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Risk input invalid");
    });
    try { result.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); }
    catch (ExecutionException error) { System.out.println(error.getCause().getMessage()); }
} finally {
    pool.shutdownNow();
}

Output

text
Risk input invalid

Why this happens

The task exception is captured by its Future and reported through ExecutionException. Reading the cause identifies the actual task failure.

1.09 Atomic updates concurrent maps and bounded queues

Concept

A thread-safe individual operation does not make a sequence of separate operations atomic. Use the API that protects the complete operation you need. A counter update, a per-symbol quote replacement and a multi-account transfer have different atomicity scopes.

Important methods

APIUse and limitation
AtomicLong.get(), set()Atomic value access under their memory semantics
incrementAndGet(), getAndIncrement(), addAndGet()Atomic single-counter updates with different return values
compareAndSet(expected,newValue)Conditional atomic update
updateAndGet(function)Atomic recomputation; function may be retried, so avoid side effects
LongAdder.increment(), add(), sum()Contended metrics; sum is not an atomic concurrent snapshot
ConcurrentHashMap.merge()Atomic combination for one key
ConcurrentHashMap.compute()Atomic per-key decision, such as retaining the greatest quote sequence
BlockingQueue.put(), take()Blocking producer/consumer transfer
BlockingQueue.offer(), poll() and timed formsCapacity-aware insertion and retrieval
CountDownLatch.await(), countDown()Coordinate a one-shot start or completion condition
Semaphore.acquire(), release()Bound access to a scarce resource
ReentrantLock.lock(), unlock()Explicit lock; unlock in finally

A ConcurrentHashMap does not support null keys or values. Its safe individual operations do not make get()/add/put() atomic. Its iteration is weakly consistent rather than a guaranteed single-instant snapshot. An ArrayList stored inside it remains an ordinary mutable ArrayList. LongAdder is useful for high-contention statistics, while a sequence generator generally needs a different contract such as AtomicLong.

ConcurrentHashMap.merge performs a keyed atomic increment. By contrast, counts.put(symbol, counts.getOrDefault(symbol,0L)+1) consists of separate reads and writes that can lose increments.

Scenario Count work from two workers

Two workers must increment one counter without losing updates.

Input

text
Workers: 2
Increments per worker: 1000

Java

java
AtomicLong count = new AtomicLong();
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2);
try {
    Runnable work = () -> { for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) count.incrementAndGet(); };
    Future<?> first = pool.submit(work);
    Future<?> second = pool.submit(work);
    first.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    second.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
    System.out.println(count.get());
} finally {
    pool.shutdownNow();
}

Output

text
2000

Why this happens

incrementAndGet is atomic. Waiting for both futures establishes completion before the final total is checked.

Scenario Update a shared symbol count atomically

Two completed updates contribute to the AAPL counter.

Input

text
Initial map: empty
Updates: AAPL +1, AAPL +1

Java

java
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
counts.merge("AAPL", 1L, Long::sum);
counts.merge("AAPL", 1L, Long::sum);
System.out.println(counts.get("AAPL"));

Output

text
2

Why this happens

Each merge combines the current value atomically for that key. The operation remains safe when callers execute these merges concurrently.

Scenario Apply backpressure at a queue boundary

An event queue can hold only two records.

Input

text
Capacity: 2
Offers: E1, E2, E3

Java

java
BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2);
System.out.println(queue.offer("E1"));
System.out.println(queue.offer("E2"));
System.out.println(queue.offer("E3"));
System.out.println(queue.poll());

Output

text
true
true
false
E1

Why this happens

offer reports failure when the bounded queue is full. The caller must choose whether to retry, reject or otherwise handle overload.

1.10 ThreadLocal context and CompletableFuture composition

Concept and context cleanup

ThreadLocal.get(), set(), remove() and withInitial() manage a value per thread. A worker pool reuses threads, so clean per-test context in finally to prevent state leaking into the next task. Storing the same mutable object in every thread's ThreadLocal does not make that object isolated or thread-safe. An explicitly passed test context may be clearer when work crosses thread boundaries.

ThreadLocal methods

MethodMeaning
get()Read the current thread's value
set(value)Set the current thread's value
remove()Remove the current thread's stored value
withInitial(supplier)Supply an initial value separately for each thread

CompletableFuture methods

supplyAsync() starts result-producing work, thenApply() maps a result, thenCompose() chains an asynchronous result, and thenCombine() combines independent results. allOf() completes when all supplied futures complete but does not directly return their values. exceptionally() handles failure and handle() sees success or failure. join() wraps exceptional completion in unchecked CompletionException; get() uses checked exceptions including ExecutionException and InterruptedException. For blocking checks, consider an explicit appropriate executor instead of assuming the common pool suits the workload. orTimeout() times out the future's completion; it does not guarantee termination of the underlying work.

Scenario Remove task-specific context

An order ID should not remain attached to a reused worker after its task finishes.

Input

text
Context set for this task: ORDER-O1

Java

java
ThreadLocal<String> context = new ThreadLocal<>();
try {
    context.set("ORDER-O1");
    System.out.println(context.get());
} finally {
    context.remove();
}
System.out.println(context.get());

Output

text
ORDER-O1
null

Why this happens

The second read sees no stored context. In a pool, this cleanup prevents the next task on that worker from inheriting stale state.

Scenario Combine two completed risk values

Compose two simulated completed results without manually reading and adding them separately.

Input

text
Credit result: 100.25
Market result: 50.00

Java

java
CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> credit = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(new BigDecimal("100.25"));
CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> market = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(new BigDecimal("50.00"));
BigDecimal total = credit.thenCombine(market, BigDecimal::add).join();
System.out.println(total);

Output

text
150.25

Why this happens

thenCombine combines two results. These futures are already completed, so this example teaches composition; it does not itself start parallel work.

Each question is followed immediately by its available answer, explanation and related notes. Try the question first, then read the material directly beneath it. Exercises without an existing worked solution have an explicit answer-status note. The short scenarios in Part 1 can be used for revision.

For the final nine trading question-bank exercises, use this model unless the question supplies a different one:

java
enum Side { BUY, SELL }
enum Status { PENDING, EXECUTED, CANCELLED, REJECTED }
record Trade(String tradeId, String symbol, Side side, Status status,

2.01 Find duplicate trade IDs in second occurrence order

Question

Implement findDuplicateTradeIds(List<String>). Return each duplicated ID once, ordered by when its second occurrence is encountered. IDs are case-sensitive and matched exactly. Do not modify the input. Reject a null list, null ID or blank ID with IllegalArgumentException.

Example: [T1, T2, T2, T3, T1, T2] returns [T2, T1].

Answer

java
import java.math.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Main {
    public static List<String> findDuplicateTradeIds(List<String> tradeIds) {
        if (tradeIds == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Trade ID list must not be null");
        }
        Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
        List<String> duplicates = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String id : tradeIds) {
            if (id == null || id.isBlank()) {
                throw new IllegalArgumentException("Trade ID must not be null or blank");
            }
            int count = counts.getOrDefault(id, 0) + 1;
            counts.put(id, count);
            if (count == 2) {
                duplicates.add(id);
            }
        }
        return duplicates;
    }

    private static int checks;

    private static void check(boolean condition, String description) {
        checks++;
        if (!condition) throw new AssertionError(description);
    }

    private static void rejects(Runnable action) {
        checks++;
        try {
            action.run();
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
            return;
        }
        throw new AssertionError("Expected IllegalArgumentException");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> input = Arrays.asList("T1", "T2", "T2", "T3", "T1", "T2");
        List<String> before = new ArrayList<>(input);
        check(findDuplicateTradeIds(input).equals(List.of("T2", "T1")), "Second occurrence ordering");
        check(input.equals(before), "Input remains unchanged");
        check(findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of()).isEmpty(), "Empty input");
        check(findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of("T1", "T2")).isEmpty(), "Unique IDs");
        check(findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of("T1", "T1", "T1")).equals(List.of("T1")), "Output once");
        check(findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of("T1", "t1", "t1", "T1")).equals(List.of("t1", "T1")), "Case sensitivity");
        rejects(() -> findDuplicateTradeIds(null));
        rejects(() -> findDuplicateTradeIds(Arrays.asList("T1", null)));
        rejects(() -> findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of("")));
        rejects(() -> findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of(" ")));
        System.out.println(findDuplicateTradeIds(input));
        System.out.println("PASS: " + checks + " checks");
    }
}

Detailed explanation

Step 1 Validate before iterating

Reject a null list before the enhanced for-loop. For every element, check null before isBlank so the method call is safe.

Step 2 Choose separate state for counting and output

The HashMap answers how often an ID has occurred. The ArrayList records when each duplicate becomes eligible for output. Those are different responsibilities.

Step 3 Read update and store the count

getOrDefault(id, 0) reads the current count or zero. Add one and store it using put; getOrDefault alone does not change the map.

Step 4 Append exactly at the second occurrence

count == 2 identifies the first time an ID becomes a duplicate. count > 1 would append it again at the third and later occurrences.

Step 5 Return the list built during the scan

Appending during the input scan preserves second-occurrence order. Iterating a HashMap of final counts would not preserve that order.

Walkthrough with input and output

Input IDUpdated countResult so far
T11[]
T21[]
T22[T2]
T31[T2]
T12[T2, T1]
T23[T2, T1]

Edge cases and tests

An empty or all-unique input returns an empty list. Repeated copies of one ID appear once. Case and surrounding nonblank characters are matched exactly. The input list remains unchanged.

Additional explanation and complexity

The map stores a count for each ID. getOrDefault(id, 0) returns zero for a new ID. Add one, store the new count and append the ID only when the count reaches two. Third and later occurrences do not append another result. Appending during the input scan preserves the required ordering.

HashMap iteration order is not guaranteed. Counting everything and then filtering the map cannot recover second-occurrence order by itself. A LinkedHashMap of counts would preserve first insertion order, which is a different rule.

Complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(k) additional space for k distinct IDs.

Corrections discussed

  • java.util.* does not import Collectors from the java.util.stream subpackage.
  • A stream of map entries collects entries unless you map each entry to its key.
  • An unused result-list variable should be removed or used.
  • A frequency map can identify duplicates, but output ordering must be designed explicitly.

Source file: programs/01-duplicate-trade-ids/Main.java

2.02 Duplicate IDs using Streams

Question

Solve the same duplicate-ID problem with Streams while retaining second-occurrence order.

Answer

java
import java.math.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Main {
    public static List<String> findDuplicateTradeIds(List<String> tradeIds) {
        if (tradeIds == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("List must not be null");
        }
        if (tradeIds.stream().anyMatch(id -> id == null || id.isBlank())) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("IDs must not be null or blank");
        }
        List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(tradeIds);
        Map<String, List<Integer>> positions = IntStream.range(0, ids.size())
                .boxed()
                .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(ids::get));

        return positions.entrySet().stream()
                .filter(entry -> entry.getValue().size() > 1)
                .sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(entry -> entry.getValue().get(1)))
                .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
                .collect(Collectors.toList());
    }

    private static int checks;

    private static void check(boolean condition, String description) {
        checks++;
        if (!condition) throw new AssertionError(description);
    }

    private static void rejects(Runnable action) {
        checks++;
        try {
            action.run();
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
            return;
        }
        throw new AssertionError("Expected IllegalArgumentException");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        check(findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of("T1", "T2", "T2", "T3", "T1", "T2"))
                .equals(List.of("T2", "T1")), "Second occurrence order");
        check(findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of()).isEmpty(), "Empty input");
        check(findDuplicateTradeIds(new LinkedList<>(List.of("B", "A", "A", "B")))
                .equals(List.of("A", "B")), "LinkedList input");
        check(findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of("A", "A", "A")).equals(List.of("A")), "One output per ID");
        rejects(() -> findDuplicateTradeIds(null));
        rejects(() -> findDuplicateTradeIds(Arrays.asList("T1", null)));
        rejects(() -> findDuplicateTradeIds(List.of(" ")));
        System.out.println("PASS: " + checks + " checks");
    }
}

Detailed explanation

Step 1 Validate the input

Reject null or blank IDs before grouping. The preliminary anyMatch stops as soon as invalid data is found.

Step 2 Copy for predictable indexed access

The ArrayList copy makes ids.get(index) efficient even when the supplied list is a LinkedList.

Step 3 Generate and group positions

IntStream.range generates indexes from zero to size minus one. boxed turns primitive indexes into Integer objects. groupingBy(ids::get) uses the ID at each index as the group key.

Step 4 Keep groups with a duplicate

A positions list of size greater than one identifies a duplicated ID. The second position is get(1), because list indexes start at zero.

Step 5 Sort before extracting IDs

The comparator orders entries by the second position. map(Map.Entry::getKey) then changes a stream of map entries into a stream of Strings.

Step 6 Collect the ordered result

The terminal collector executes the pipeline and returns the list. This approach trades additional memory and sorting for a stream-based description.

Walkthrough with input and output

IDEncounter positionsSecond position
T1[0, 4]4
T2[1, 2, 5]2
T3[3]Not duplicated

Sorting eligible entries by the second position produces [T2, T1].

Edge cases and tests

Empty input produces no groups. A repeated ID still produces one group. The example deliberately avoids a stateful external HashSet inside filter; the shorter shortcut is retained only as a caution in the original explanation.

Additional explanation and complexity

IntStream generates input indexes. groupingBy associates each ID with its ordered list of positions. Keep IDs with at least two positions, sort by position number two, then return the keys. For the main example, T1 has positions [0, 4], while T2 has [1, 2, 5]. T2's second position is earlier.

Copying the input to an ArrayList ensures efficient indexed access even if the caller supplied a LinkedList. Compared with the loop, this approach stores more information and sorts the duplicated IDs.

A shorter sequential shortcut was also discussed:

java
Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
List<String> duplicates = tradeIds.stream()
        .filter(id -> !seen.add(id))
        .distinct()
        .collect(Collectors.toList());

This shortcut assumes valid input and sequential execution. Its predicate mutates external state, which Java's stream guidance discourages. Do not switch it to parallel execution. Prefer the loop or the index-based version when discussing clear, maintainable interview code.

Complexity: O(n + d log d) expected time for d duplicated IDs, and O(n) additional space.

Source file: programs/02-duplicate-ids-streams/Main.java

2.03 Validate a trading order and return all errors

Question

Implement validateOrder(symbol, quantity, price). Return every validation error in symbol, quantity, price order. Symbol must not be null or blank; quantity must be positive; price must be non-null and positive. Return an empty list for a valid order. Invalid values produce messages rather than exceptions.

Answer

java
import java.math.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Main {
    public static List<String> validateOrder(String symbol, int quantity, BigDecimal price) {
        List<String> errors = new ArrayList<>();
        if (symbol == null || symbol.isBlank()) {
            errors.add("Symbol is required");
        }
        if (quantity <= 0) {
            errors.add("Quantity must be positive");
        }
        if (price == null || price.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0) {
            errors.add("Price must be positive");
        }
        return errors;
    }

    private static int checks;

    private static void check(boolean condition, String description) {
        checks++;
        if (!condition) throw new AssertionError(description);
    }

    private static void rejects(Runnable action) {
        checks++;
        try {
            action.run();
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
            return;
        }
        throw new AssertionError("Expected IllegalArgumentException");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        check(validateOrder("AAPL", 100, new BigDecimal("150.50")).isEmpty(), "Valid order");
        check(validateOrder("", 0, new BigDecimal("-10")).equals(List.of(
                "Symbol is required", "Quantity must be positive", "Price must be positive")), "All errors");
        check(validateOrder("AAPL", 10, null).equals(List.of("Price must be positive")), "Null price");
        check(validateOrder(null, -1, BigDecimal.ZERO).size() == 3, "All invalid boundaries");
        check(validateOrder(" ", 1, BigDecimal.ONE).equals(List.of("Symbol is required")), "Blank symbol");
        System.out.println("PASS: " + checks + " checks");
    }
}

Detailed explanation

Step 1 Create a result list

This method returns validation findings. It does not throw for ordinary invalid field values because the caller needs all errors together.

Step 2 Check the symbol

A null symbol and a blank symbol both add the same business message. Short-circuit OR protects the isBlank call.

Step 3 Check quantity independently

quantity <= 0 rejects both zero and negatives. This is a separate if, so an invalid symbol does not prevent a quantity error from being recorded.

Step 4 Check the decimal price

A null price is rejected before comparison. compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) <= 0 means the price is numerically zero or negative.

Step 5 Return errors in rule order

Messages are added in symbol, quantity, price order. A valid order adds nothing and therefore returns an empty list.

Walkthrough with input and output

FieldInputDecision
Symbolempty stringAdd Symbol is required
Quantity0Add Quantity must be positive
Price-10Add Price must be positive

All three messages are returned, in that order.

Edge cases and tests

Test each invalid field alone, all invalid fields together, null price, blank symbol and the exact zero boundaries. Using else-if or printing instead of adding messages would violate the output contract.

Additional explanation and complexity

Each independent if statement checks one field and appends a message. Using else-if would stop later checks when an earlier field is invalid. A null price must be checked before calling compareTo(). The OR expression short-circuits, so compareTo() is skipped when the value is null.

This validation function intentionally collects errors. A constructor in a later exercise intentionally throws an exception instead: the two contracts serve different purposes.

Complexity: O(1) field checks, plus the cost of examining the symbol text.

Corrections discussed

  • this cannot be used in a static method. Parameters already contain the input values.
  • Objects.requireNonNull() throws NullPointerException; it does not collect validation messages.
  • BigDecimal cannot be compared with <=; use compareTo().
  • List is an interface. Instantiate ArrayList, not new List<String>().
  • System.out.println() prints a message; errors.add() includes it in the returned result.
  • Java keywords are case-sensitive: if is valid; If is not.

2.04 Calculate total trade quantity by symbol

Question

Given Trade objects containing symbol and quantity, return Map<String, Integer> with the total quantity for each symbol. Do not modify the input. Return an empty map for an empty list. Inputs are valid and totals fit in int.

Answer

java
import java.math.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Main {
    static class Trade {
        final String symbol;
        final int quantity;
        Trade(String symbol, int quantity) {
            this.symbol = symbol;
            this.quantity = quantity;
        }
    }

    public static Map<String, Integer> totalQuantityBySymbol(List<Trade> trades) {
        Map<String, Integer> totals = new HashMap<>();
        for (Trade trade : trades) {
            totals.put(trade.symbol,
                    totals.getOrDefault(trade.symbol, 0) + trade.quantity);
        }
        return totals;
    }

    private static int checks;

    private static void check(boolean condition, String description) {
        checks++;
        if (!condition) throw new AssertionError(description);
    }

    private static void rejects(Runnable action) {
        checks++;
        try {
            action.run();
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
            return;
        }
        throw new AssertionError("Expected IllegalArgumentException");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<Trade> trades = List.of(new Trade("AAPL", 100), new Trade("MSFT", 50),
                new Trade("AAPL", 200), new Trade("MSFT", 25), new Trade("GOOG", 10));
        check(totalQuantityBySymbol(trades).equals(Map.of("AAPL", 300, "MSFT", 75, "GOOG", 10)), "Totals");
        check(totalQuantityBySymbol(List.of()).isEmpty(), "Empty input");
        check(totalQuantityBySymbol(List.of(new Trade("AAPL", 5))).get("AAPL") == 5, "Single trade");
        System.out.println(totalQuantityBySymbol(trades));
        System.out.println("PASS: " + checks + " checks");
    }
}

Detailed explanation

Step 1 Initialise a fresh map

The method name is not a map variable. totals is the local map that will store one running quantity per symbol.

Step 2 Read one trade at a time

The enhanced for-loop gives access to that trade’s symbol and quantity. No sorting or input modification is necessary.

Step 3 Default a new symbol to zero

getOrDefault(symbol, 0) means the same update works for a first trade and for subsequent trades.

Step 4 Add the current quantity

Add trade.quantity to the current accumulated number, then put the updated number under the same symbol.

Step 5 Return the map

The output has one total for every observed symbol. HashMap output order is unspecified and is not part of this exercise’s contract.

Walkthrough with input and output

TradePrevious totalNew total
AAPL 1000AAPL 100
MSFT 500MSFT 50
AAPL 200100AAPL 300
MSFT 2550MSFT 75

Edge cases and tests

Empty input returns an empty map. Repeated symbols must add rather than replace their quantities. The original exercise assumes totals fit in int; discuss long, exact overflow checks or another representation if that guarantee changes.

Additional explanation and complexity

The map has one entry per symbol. Get the current quantity, default to zero when the symbol is new, add the trade's quantity and put the updated value back into the map.

java
int currentTotal = totals.getOrDefault(trade.symbol, 0);
int updatedTotal = currentTotal + trade.quantity;
totals.put(trade.symbol, updatedTotal);

For AAPL quantities 100 and 200, the updates are 0 + 100 = 100, then 100 + 200 = 300. getOrDefault() itself does not change the map; put() stores the result. If a key explicitly maps to null, getOrDefault() returns null rather than the default; this counting implementation never stores null values.

A follow-up asked for a merge() rewrite. It was posed as an exercise in the chat rather than worked through there.

Complexity: Expected O(n) time and O(k) space for k symbols.

Corrections discussed

  • The method name totalQuantityBySymbol is not a map variable. Declare a result map such as totals.
  • Map.get(symbol) returns the quantity, not a symbol string. Comparing that Integer to trade.symbol is incorrect.
  • No contains check is required when getOrDefault() handles new symbols.

2.05 Find the trade with the highest quantity

Question

Return the Trade object with the highest quantity. Preserve the first encountered object on a tie. Return null for an empty list. Do not sort or modify the input. The list and its elements are non-null.

Answer

java
import java.math.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Main {
    static class Trade {
        final String symbol;
        final int quantity;
        Trade(String symbol, int quantity) {
            this.symbol = symbol;
            this.quantity = quantity;
        }
    }

    public static Trade findLargestTrade(List<Trade> trades) {
        Trade largest = null;
        for (Trade trade : trades) {
            if (largest == null || trade.quantity > largest.quantity) {
                largest = trade;
            }
        }
        return largest;
    }

    private static int checks;

    private static void check(boolean condition, String description) {
        checks++;
        if (!condition) throw new AssertionError(description);
    }

    private static void rejects(Runnable action) {
        checks++;
        try {
            action.run();
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
            return;
        }
        throw new AssertionError("Expected IllegalArgumentException");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Trade firstWinner = new Trade("MSFT", 250);
        Trade laterTie = new Trade("AMZN", 250);
        List<Trade> trades = List.of(new Trade("AAPL", 100), firstWinner,
                new Trade("GOOG", 150), laterTie);
        check(findLargestTrade(trades) == firstWinner, "First object wins tie");
        check(findLargestTrade(List.of()) == null, "Empty list");
        check(findLargestTrade(List.of(laterTie)) == laterTie, "Single object");
        check(findLargestTrade(List.of(new Trade("A", -10), new Trade("B", -5))).quantity == -5,
                "Algorithm does not assume a zero starting maximum");
        System.out.println(findLargestTrade(trades).symbol);
        System.out.println("PASS: " + checks + " checks");
    }
}

Detailed explanation

Step 1 Represent no winner with null

Before seeing a trade there is no winning object. Starting with null also avoids assuming quantities are greater than an arbitrary starting number.

Step 2 Accept the first trade

largest == null is true on the first iteration, so the first object becomes the current winner.

Step 3 Compare later quantities

Replace the winner only when the new quantity is strictly greater. Using >= would incorrectly keep the last tied trade.

Step 4 Keep the object reference

Storing the Trade itself preserves its symbol and associated data. It also lets the caller verify that the first original object won the tie.

Step 5 Handle an empty input naturally

No loop iteration runs for an empty list, so the method returns null as required.

Walkthrough with input and output

SymbolQuantityCurrent winner after comparison
AAPL100AAPL 100
MSFT250MSFT 250
GOOG150MSFT 250
AMZN250MSFT 250

Edge cases and tests

Test empty input, one object, a larger value at the end and tied maximum quantities. The algorithm changes only its local winning reference; it does not sort or change the list.

Additional explanation and complexity

largest begins as null because no trade has been examined. The first trade becomes the current winner. A later object replaces it only when its quantity is strictly greater. Using > instead of >= preserves the first object on equal quantities. Returning the object retains its associated symbol and other fields.

Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) additional space.

2.06 Find trades missing from actual results

Question

Return IDs present in expected but absent from actual. Preserve expected-list order. Ignore extra IDs in actual. Do not modify either list. Both inputs contain unique, non-null IDs and are non-null.

Example: expected [T1, T2, T3, T4], actual [T2, T4, T5] returns [T1, T3].

Answer

java
import java.math.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Main {
    public static List<String> findMissingTrades(List<String> expected, List<String> actual) {
        Set<String> actualTrades = new HashSet<>(actual);
        List<String> missingTrades = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String trade : expected) {
            if (!actualTrades.contains(trade)) {
                missingTrades.add(trade);
            }
        }
        return missingTrades;
    }

    private static int checks;

    private static void check(boolean condition, String description) {
        checks++;
        if (!condition) throw new AssertionError(description);
    }

    private static void rejects(Runnable action) {
        checks++;
        try {
            action.run();
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
            return;
        }
        throw new AssertionError("Expected IllegalArgumentException");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> expected = Arrays.asList("T1", "T2", "T3", "T4");
        List<String> actual = Arrays.asList("T2", "T4", "T5");
        check(findMissingTrades(expected, actual).equals(List.of("T1", "T3")), "Missing IDs");
        check(expected.equals(List.of("T1", "T2", "T3", "T4")), "Expected unchanged");
        check(actual.equals(List.of("T2", "T4", "T5")), "Actual unchanged");
        check(findMissingTrades(List.of("T1", "T2"), List.of("T2", "T1")).isEmpty(), "All present");
        check(findMissingTrades(List.of("T1", "T2"), List.of()).equals(List.of("T1", "T2")), "Actual empty");
        check(findMissingTrades(List.of(), List.of("T1")).isEmpty(), "Expected empty");
        System.out.println("PASS: " + checks + " checks");
    }
}

Detailed explanation

Step 1 Index actual IDs for membership

new HashSet<>(actual) copies the actual IDs into a set. Membership has expected constant-time cost under ordinary hashing assumptions.

Step 2 Scan expected rather than actual

The question asks what expected data is missing. Iterating actual instead would find unexpected extras, which is the opposite direction.

Step 3 Append only absent IDs

The negated contains check is true only when the actual set has no matching ID.

Step 4 Preserve encounter order

The result is appended in expected-list order. HashSet iteration order is irrelevant because the method never uses it to construct the result.

Step 5 Return a new list

The original expected and actual lists are preserved. This also works when those lists are fixed-size or unmodifiable.

Walkthrough with input and output

Expected IDIn actual [T2, T4, T5]Action
T1NoAppend T1
T2YesSkip
T3NoAppend T3
T4YesSkip

The result is [T1, T3]. Extra actual ID T5 is ignored.

Edge cases and tests

If actual is empty, every expected ID is returned. If expected is empty, the result is empty. The original inputs contain unique non-null IDs; define a duplicate policy if that changes.

Additional explanation and complexity

Create a set from actual so each membership lookup has expected constant time. Scan expected, adding only IDs that the set does not contain. The scan order preserves expected order.

java
Set<String> actualTrades = new HashSet<>(actual);

Set<String> is the variable's interface type. HashSet is its implementation. The constructor copies the input elements into the new set and removes duplicate values without modifying the original list. This is equivalent to creating an empty HashSet and calling addAll(actual).

Complexity: Expected O(n + m) time; O(m) set storage plus the output list.

Corrections discussed

  • Looping through actual and checking absence from expected answers the reverse question.
  • Add missing IDs to a new result list, not to expected.
  • Arrays.asList() returns a fixed-size list. add() and remove() are unsupported, although replacing an existing element with set() is supported.
  • Returning expected would return the original expected records rather than just the missing ones.

2.07 Check a palindrome after cleaning the string

Question

Return whether a string reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring letter case and ordinary spaces. Return false for null and true for the empty string. Inputs contain English letters and ordinary spaces.

Answer

java
import java.math.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class Main {
    public static boolean isPalindrome(String text) {
        if (text == null) return false;
        String cleaned = text.replace(" ", "").toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
        int left = 0;
        int right = cleaned.length() - 1;
        while (left < right) {
            if (cleaned.charAt(left) != cleaned.charAt(right)) return false;
            left++;
            right--;
        }
        return true;
    }

    private static int checks;

    private static void check(boolean condition, String description) {
        checks++;
        if (!condition) throw new AssertionError(description);
    }

    private static void rejects(Runnable action) {
        checks++;
        try {
            action.run();
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) {
            return;
        }
        throw new AssertionError("Expected IllegalArgumentException");
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] inputs = {"madam", "Race car", "Never odd or even", "Java", "", null, "   ", "a", "ab"};
        boolean[] expected = {true, true, true, false, true, false, true, true, false};
        for (int i = 0; i < inputs.length; i++) {
            check(isPalindrome(inputs[i]) == expected[i], "Palindrome input: " + inputs[i]);
        }
        System.out.println("PASS: " + checks + " checks");
    }
}

Detailed explanation

Step 1 Apply the null contract first

Return false before invoking any String methods when text is null.

Step 2 Normalise only what the question permits

Remove ordinary spaces and convert English letters to lower case with Locale.ROOT. Punctuation removal and full Unicode case folding are outside this exercise.

Step 3 Place indexes at opposite ends

left starts at zero and right at length minus one. charAt retrieves the character at the current position.

Step 4 Stop at the first mismatch

If a pair differs, the complete string cannot be a palindrome, so return false immediately.

Step 5 Move inward after a match

Increment left and decrement right. When they meet or cross, every required pair matched and the result is true.

Walkthrough with input and output

Cleaned textCompared positionsCharacters
racecar0 and 6r and r
racecar1 and 5a and a
racecar2 and 4c and c

The middle e needs no partner. Result: true.

Edge cases and tests

The empty string and a space-only string normalise to empty and return true. A one-character string returns true. Java is rejected at the first unequal outside pair. The cleaned copy accounts for the additional O(n) space.

Additional explanation and complexity

Remove ordinary spaces and convert letters to lower case. Compare the first and last characters, then move both indexes inward. Return false at the first mismatch. When all pairs match, return true. An empty cleaned string skips the loop.

charAt(index) retrieves a character. This exercise intentionally does not define full Unicode case folding or punctuation removal.

Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) additional space for the cleaned string.
